issues.explanation: Pregnancy/birth/babies reminders are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness. For this trauma type, child-health, hospital, medical, or illness-related cues would be expected; pregnancy/childbirth cues imply a different trauma context unless there is additional undisclosed perinatal trauma.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
issues.explanation: The appraisal that 'nothing has been done about it' fits neglect, betrayal, or preventable harm more than a child's serious illness. In the context of a life-threatening illness, the unfairness element is plausible, but the added idea that nothing has been done is clinically discordant unless there was clear medical negligence, which is not otherwise reflected in the profile.

Alcohol smell is not well aligned with the stated trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness, while the other trigger items are strongly medical/hospital-based. Without any corroborating trauma content suggesting alcohol was central to the child's illness experience, this item looks clinically out of place within the trigger set.

issues.item: Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
issues.explanation: 'Cannot trust safety' suggests a pervasive current danger appraisal more typical of interpersonal violence, combat, or repeated external threat. For a trauma centered on a child's life-threatening illness, this can occur, but here it is not well supported by the rest of the profile, which is focused on medical reminders and reliving rather than generalized danger.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: Sleep vigilance because one 'need[s] to stay alert' implies ongoing monitoring for imminent threat. In the context of a child's past life-threatening illness, this is difficult to reconcile unless there is corresponding material about night-time monitoring, medical deterioration, or responsibility for detecting danger, which is absent from the selected items.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: The hospital/medical trigger pattern fits a child's life-threatening illness, but a burnt-smell danger cue is hard to reconcile with that trauma context unless there is specific unreported trauma-related meaning. As selected, it stands out as clinically implausible relative to the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
issues.explanation: The olfactory memory item implies the original trauma involved a distinctive smell that is re-experienced. In this profile, the only corroborating smell tied to the trauma context should be hospital/antiseptic cues; pairing it with a burnt-smell trigger creates an incoherent sensory trauma context for a child's medical illness.

vignette: Rohan, a 58-year-old South Asian man, had spent his career as a bomb disposal technician, a job that required precision and calm under pressure. However, it wasn't an explosion or a near-miss that brought him to therapy - it was the memory of his young daughter's life-threatening illness several years ago. Rohan recalled the hospital's antiseptic smell, which still made him queasy to this day. Even the sight of medical equipment like needles and drips would transport him back to those anxious days. When Rohan found himself in a situation that triggered these memories - such as being around children or catching a whiff of that distinct hospital scent - he would become hypervigilant, his senses on high alert. His body would tense up, and his mind would start racing with worst-case scenarios. He couldn't shake the feeling that something terrible was lurking just beneath the surface, waiting to pounce. This state of heightened arousal made it impossible for him to fall asleep at night; he needed to stay alert, just in case. These physical reactions were so intense that Rohan began to wonder if he was losing his grip on reality. He felt weak and helpless, unable to protect himself or those he loved from the dangers that seemed to lurk around every corner. The memories of his daughter's illness would come flooding back without warning, triggered by something as mundane as a hospital smell or the sight of medical equipment. When this happened, Rohan would relive the experience in vivid detail - the beeping machines, the antiseptic tang, the desperate feeling of being unable to do anything to help. As these memories resurfaced, Rohan's negative appraisals of himself grew stronger. He believed that he was a weak person, incapable of coping with stress or protecting those around him. This fear of going crazy - of losing control completely - only added to his sense of helplessness. The more he struggled to push these thoughts away, the more they seemed to cling to him. Rohan's work as a bomb disposal technician began to suffer as well. He found himself avoiding situations that might trigger these memories or emotions, opting instead for safer, less demanding tasks. His relationships with his colleagues and family members also started to fray; he became withdrawn and isolated, unable to shake the feeling that he was a burden to those around him. One day, while working on a particularly difficult disposal operation, Rohan caught a whiff of something that smelled eerily like hospital antiseptic. Suddenly, he was back in that hospital room, reliving the terror and helplessness all over again. His body tensed up, his mind racing with worst-case scenarios - and in that moment, Rohan knew he needed help. As he sat in therapy for the first time, Rohan's eyes darted around the room, searching for potential threats or triggers. He fidgeted with his hands, his body still on high alert from years of sleepless nights and hypervigilance. But as he began to talk about his experiences - about the memories that haunted him and the fears that gripped him - Rohan started to realize that he wasn't alone in this fight. He was taking the first tentative steps towards confronting those negative appraisals, towards relearning how to live with himself and his memories. And though it wouldn't be easy, Rohan knew that he had to try - for himself, and for those around him who cared about him most.
